title: Examples and Output Contracts
summary: Use representative examples and explicit output contracts to make responses easier to consume and validate.
objectives: Choose examples that demonstrate desired behavior without hiding the governing rule.
Define a human-readable or machine-readable output contract.
Distinguish requested formatting, valid JSON, and schema-constrained output.
Validate content and edge cases after structural parsing succeeds.

sections.title: Examples demonstrate a pattern
paragraphs: Examples can show tone, classification boundaries, field population, and how unusual inputs should be handled. They work best when the desired rule is also stated explicitly. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Choose relevant and varied examples. Repeating one easy case can teach an accidental pattern and conceal how the task should behave at its boundaries. sections.callout: An example illustrates the rule; it should not be the only place the rule exists.

sections.title: Define the output before generating it
paragraphs: An output contract names the fields or sections, allowed values, required evidence, ordering, length, and behavior when data is unknown. This makes the response easier for a person or application to inspect. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

For prose, a heading template or table may be enough. For application data, use a supported structured-output or schema mechanism when the provider offers one instead of relying only on instructions to produce JSON. code.label: Provider-neutral output-contract template
code.code:
Deliverable purpose: [WHO USES IT AND WHY]
Format: [PROSE, TABLE, OR NAMED SCHEMA]
Required fields/sections: [LIST]
Allowed values: [ENUMS OR RULES]
Evidence: [CITATIONS, QUOTES, TESTS, OR NONE]
Unknown values: [NULL, OMIT, OR EXPLAIN]
Ordering and limits: [RULES]
Validation: [PARSER/SCHEMA PLUS CONTENT CHECKS]

sections.title: Formatting, valid data, and schema adherence differ
paragraphs: A prompt can request a layout, but the response may still vary. JSON mode or an equivalent feature can require syntactically valid JSON without guaranteeing that every required field and type matches your contract. Schema-constrained output is designed to enforce a supported schema. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Provider capabilities and supported schema subsets vary. Keep the portable contract separate from provider-specific API configuration, and test the exact model and interface you deploy. sections.title: A valid shape can still contain a bad answer
paragraphs: Parsing proves structure, not factual correctness, completeness, authorization, or usefulness. Validate required business rules, source support, allowed values, cross-field consistency, and downstream consequences. Handle refusals, incomplete output, missing data, and validation errors explicitly. Never convert a parse failure into fabricated default values that look authoritative. activity.title: Design and test an output contract
instructions: Choose a recurring task such as issue triage, meeting-summary extraction, or product comparison.
Define purpose, required fields, allowed values, evidence, unknown-value behavior, ordering, and validation.
Create three examples: a normal case, a boundary case, and a case with missing information.
Review a sample response twice—first for structure, then for factual and business-rule correctness.
evidence: A completed output contract and three varied input/output examples.
A two-part validation checklist separating structural checks from content and consequence checks.
activity.reflectionPrompt: What error would pass your structural validation but still make the result unsafe or useless?

cues.text: Explain how diverse normal, boundary, and missing-data examples reveal the intended rule.
Show a three-column grid for normal, boundary, and missing-data examples, each linked to the rule it demonstrates.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A text table lists three example types—normal, boundary, and missing data—and the rule each is meant to demonstrate. Reduced-motion mode displays the full table.

cues.text: Build the provider-neutral contract from purpose through validation and distinguish human from application consumers.
Ask learners to choose an explicit representation for unknown values instead of allowing silent invention.
Allow two minutes to define required fields and unknown-value behavior.
Contrast requested formatting, valid JSON, and supported schema adherence without implying that every provider implements them identically.
Separate parser success from factual, business-rule, authorization, and consequence checks.
Check that learners can name one schema-valid but factually invalid response.
Guide learners through building the contract and reviewing the same output for structure and content separately.
Begin the check after the contract handles boundary, missing-data, refusal, and invalid-content cases.

questions.prompt: Which example set teaches a classification boundary most effectively?
choices: Relevant normal, boundary, and missing-information cases tied to an explicit rule
Three nearly identical easy cases
One example with no explanation
Only examples that produce the same label
questions.explanation: Varied examples expose boundaries while the explicit rule prevents accidental imitation.

questions.prompt: What belongs in an output contract?
choices: Only a request to be concise
The model's private reasoning
Required structure, allowed values, evidence, unknown handling, and validation
A guarantee that all facts are current
questions.explanation: These elements make the deliverable inspectable and consumable.

questions.prompt: What does syntactically valid JSON prove?
choices: Every field matches the intended schema
The data can be parsed as JSON, but content and schema still require checking unless separately enforced
Every factual claim is correct
The response is authorized for automatic action
questions.explanation: Syntax, schema adherence, content correctness, and authorization are distinct checks.

questions.prompt: What should an application do when a structured response is refused or incomplete?
choices: Invent missing required fields
Retry forever
Skip content validation
Handle the condition explicitly and avoid treating it as validated data
questions.explanation: Refusals and incomplete responses are expected branches and must not become fabricated records.

questions.prompt: A response matches its schema but cites the wrong source. What is true?
choices: The structure passed, but the evidence and factual validation failed
The response is valid because parsing succeeded
The schema should be removed
No review is needed
questions.explanation: Schema validation cannot establish that a claim is supported by the cited evidence.
